intro: This guide takes your group through Mary Slessor (For Teens) in thirteen weeks, one chapter a week. It’s written for teens aged about 13 to 18 and works well for a youth group, a homeschool or a small group. It follows Mary from a Dundee tenement and a weaving loom to Calabar and the forests of Okoyong in West Africa, where she spent nearly forty years rescuing twins, standing against killings and loving people others had thrown away. It tells her story honestly, including her temper, her mistakes and the colonial power that stood behind her.

Each session takes about 30 to 40 minutes. Open by saying the memory verse together (3 minutes). Read the chapter, either aloud together or at home beforehand (5–10 minutes). Talk through the chapter’s three questions, which come with answers to help you (10–15 minutes). Do the activity (10 minutes). Then close in prayer (2–3 minutes), in your own words or by turning the chapter’s closing “One thing to do this week” into a prayer together, and leave that challenge with the group for the week ahead.

To prepare, read the chapter yourself first and look over the activity; most weeks need only paper and pens, or nothing at all. This book includes a father’s drinking and a family’s poverty, the killing and abandonment of twin babies, poison ordeals and killings at funerals, the deaths of many children and of Mary’s own family, and a long season of grief that may have been depression. Some teens may recognise their own homes in Mary’s Saturday nights, so keep reflection private, never press anyone to share, and follow up gently with anyone who seems affected. Be ready to point them to a parent, pastor, teacher, doctor or other trusted adult, as the chapters themselves do.

weeks.summary: Mary grows up in Aberdeen and Dundee with a gentle, praying mother who follows every report of the Calabar mission, and a father who drinks away the family’s money. On Saturday nights mother and daughter sew and wait for his unsteady footsteps, and Mary prays for him for years without seeing him change before he dies in 1870. The big idea: our heavenly Father pities our weakness, and we can leave our unanswered prayers with him.

memory_verse.text: As a father shows compassion to his children, so the LORD shows compassion to those who fear him.

activity.title: Leave It with Him
steps: Read Mary’s words aloud: “I know my heavenly Father so well that I can leave it with Him for the lower fatherhood.”
Discuss the difference between giving up on a prayer and leaving it with God.
Have each person write privately one prayer they have prayed for a long time without an answer, with “I can leave it with Him” underneath.
Repeat plainly what the chapter says: a family’s hidden trouble is not your fault and not your job to keep secret, and anyone who isn’t safe at home should tell a trusted adult.

weeks.summary: At eleven Mary goes to work at Baxter Brothers’ mill, becomes a skilled weaver, and by twenty-one is head of her household in all but name after her brothers and father die. She reads with a book propped on her loom, teaches rough boys at a church mission, and, by her own later telling, stands her ground when a gang leader swings a lead weight at her head. The big idea: courage is not the absence of fear, and a heavy load carried young can grow something good in us.

memory_verse.text: It is good for a man that he bear the yoke in his youth.

activity.title: This Is for You
steps: As a group, list the heavy or dull jobs teenagers carry: chores, caring for siblings, part-time work, study.
Read the line “Her courage was not the absence of fear. It was staying put when she wanted to run,” and discuss what it means.
Talk about Mary’s honesty that she couldn’t meditate, and her friend’s advice to go and work instead.
Have each person pick one heavy job for this week and write a one-sentence offering of it to God, such as “This is for you.”

weeks.summary: The Calabar mission began with freed Christians in Jamaica and an invitation from the Efik rulers of Calabar. After her brother John dies, Mary decides to take his place, calling Calabar the post of danger and therefore the post of honour, and in 1876 she sails, watching casks of spirits loaded aboard: “Scores of casks! And only one missionary!” The big idea: you don’t need to feel ready or fearless to say “Here I am,” only to know how much God has done for you.

memory_verse.text: And I heard the voice of the Lord saying, “Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?” Then I said, “Here I am! Send me.”

activity.title: Here I Am
steps: Read Isaiah 6:1–8 aloud and point out that Isaiah sees God’s holiness and is forgiven before he says “Here I am.”
Discuss why the chapter says Mary wasn’t a heroine when she said yes.
As a group, brainstorm small places God might send a teenager this week: a lonely classmate, a neighbour, a younger sibling.
Have each person write down one small thing they will do, and pray Isaiah’s words over it.

weeks.summary: In Calabar Mary meets an ordered Efik society with its own law, poison ordeals and killings at funerals, learns Efik by ear, and quietly sends most of her salary home. A man asks why Christian countries bring rum if it is bad, and she cannot answer him. At Old Town she confronts the killing of twins, rescues a pair, loses the boy to his relatives, and takes the girl, Janie, home to Scotland. The big idea: the one who trusts God does not need to rush, because the best things often grow slowly.

memory_verse.text: Whoever believes will not be in haste.

activity.title: Slow Growth
steps: As a group, list things that can’t be rushed: friendships, skills, trust, learning a language.
Discuss why Mary wrote this verse as a reminder to herself, and why a law against killing twins didn’t change people’s beliefs overnight.
Talk about the rum seller’s question: how can a Christian’s life back up, or undercut, what they say?
Have each person write privately one thing they are impatient about and one faithful step they can take this week.

weeks.summary: Back in Scotland Mary cares for baby Janie and provides alone for her mother and her sick sister, and her mother gives her back to God for wherever he sends her. Within weeks of Mary’s sailing again, her mother dies and then her sister, and she writes that she is “stranded and alone,” yet free to go up-country. Her house in Creek Town fills with rescued children, and the mission sends her to Okoyong. The big idea: when our flesh and heart fail, God is still the strength of our heart.

memory_verse.text: My flesh and my heart may fail, but God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever.

activity.title: We Remember
steps: Discuss the chapter’s point that grieving people often feel everyone else has moved on.
As a group, list simple ways to show a grieving person you remember: a message on a hard anniversary, saying the name of the one they lost, a visit.
Have each person write privately the name of someone who has lost a person they love, even long ago.
Encourage them to send that person a short message this week.
Remind the group that if grief ever turns into feeling they can’t go on, they should tell a safe person or call a crisis line.

weeks.summary: Okoyong is forest country where people accused of witchcraft face the poison ordeal and killings follow a chief’s death. In August 1888 Mary sets out with five children, and facing the dark forest, too afraid even to move her lips in prayer, she manages one word inside: “Father!” She goes back alone through the forest that night to fetch the loads, and her first victory saves a young slave’s life, though he is still chained and beaten. The big idea: God is with us wherever we go, so we can walk on afraid but not alone.

memory_verse.text: Have I not commanded you? Be strong and courageous. Do not be frightened, and do not be dismayed, for the LORD your God is with you wherever you go.

activity.title: One-Word Prayers
steps: Ask the group when they feel too anxious or tired to pray in full sentences.
Read Romans 8:15 aloud, where the Spirit teaches us to cry “Abba! Father!”, and connect it to Mary’s one-word prayer.
As a group, list other short prayers for moments of pressure, such as “Help,” “Thank you” or “Lord, have mercy.”
Discuss why the chapter calls most of Mary’s victories in Okoyong “real, and only partial.”
Challenge everyone to pray “Father” the next time they are anxious this week, and then take the next step.

weeks.summary: Living in one crowded room of Chief Edem’s compound, Mary prays aloud while hacking at the undergrowth with a machete so no one can hear. The chief’s sister, Ma Eme, becomes her secret ally, risking her life to warn Mary of planned killings, and their friendship lasts twenty-five years, though Ma Eme never becomes a Christian. The big idea: we can hold firmly to Christ and still honour the real kindness of friends who don’t share our faith.

memory_verse.text: A friend loves at all times, and a brother is born for adversity.

activity.title: Who Was a Neighbour?
steps: Read the parable of the Good Samaritan in Luke 10:30–37 aloud.
Discuss how Ma Eme is like the Samaritan in Jesus’ story.
Talk about the hard choice Mary made to stay silent about a killing in order to protect Ma Eme, and whether the group thinks she was right.
Have each person think of someone outside their faith who has been kind to them, and one specific thing to thank them for this week.

weeks.summary: When Chief Edem’s son Etim dies after an accident, the witch-doctor blames a nearby village and more than a dozen people are brought back in chains to face the poison ordeal. Mary sits at the gate and will not move, whispers “Ifehe!” (“Run”) to a woman about to drink and runs with her, and little by little the prisoners are released, so Etim is buried without human sacrifice. Edem later tells her many are weary of the old customs but no one can break them alone. The big idea: God calls us to rescue the weak, and one person who refuses to move can free others to stop too.

memory_verse.text: Rescue the weak and the needy; deliver them from the hand of the wicked.

activity.title: Hold the Gate
steps: Read Edem’s words: “We are all weary of the old customs, but no single person or House among us has power to break them off.”
As a group, name situations where people go along with something wrong because everyone else does, such as a group-chat pile-on, teasing or leaving someone out.
In small groups, role-play one of these, with one person practising a calm, simple way to say no or to stand with the person being targeted.
Discuss how Mary gave the people of Okoyong someone to blame (“Ma won’t let us”), and how we can make it easier for others to stop.

weeks.summary: Mary’s house becomes a refuge for abandoned babies; many die and are buried near her home, but some live, like a girl left five days in the bush. She carries the twins of Iye, a slave woman driven from her village, and raises the surviving girl, Susie, who dies at fourteen months after a terrible accident; Mary buys Iye’s freedom, and years later Iye is baptised. The big idea: even when people abandon us, the Lord takes us in, often through someone willing to carry the box.

memory_verse.text: For my father and my mother have forsaken me, but the LORD will take me in.

activity.title: Carry the Box
steps: Discuss why nobody else would touch the gin-case, and what it cost Mary to carry it.
Reread the chapter’s correction of the myth that Mary ended the killing of twins, and ask why it matters to tell the story accurately.
As a group, list the kinds of people who get avoided in a typical school or neighbourhood, without naming anyone.
Have each person decide privately on one practical way to stand with someone others avoid this week.

weeks.summary: Mary becomes engaged to Charles Morrison, but she will not leave Okoyong, the mission Board will not send him there, and they never marry. Then four of her children die, smallpox sweeps the region, and she nurses Chief Edem until he dies and buries him with her own hands; for a while she has “no heart for anything,” and after seven years she has no baptisms to report. The big idea: offering ourselves to God as a living sacrifice is costly, and we can be honest about the cost.

memory_verse.text: I appeal to you therefore, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God, which is your spiritual worship.

activity.title: Results Belong to God
steps: Read Mary’s words: “Christ sent me to preach the Gospel, and He will look after results.”
Discuss what it would be like to work hard for seven years with no visible results.
Talk about the saying that Mary was “married to Africa,” and why the chapter tells the plainer truth instead.
Have each person write privately one thing they are holding back from God, and pray, “I lay it in your hands.”
Remind the group that feeling “no heart for anything” for weeks is not a spiritual failure, and to tell a trusted person if that is them.

weeks.summary: Mary walks through drenching rain to treat a dying chief, and later, when told a woman going into a war only proves her ignorance, replies that he has forgotten “the woman’s God”; the chief she healed kneels to ask her to make peace. She runs a native court and later sits as a magistrate to protect women, but her justice is sometimes rough, and she lives with the tension that British guns stand behind her. The big idea: God requires justice, kindness and humility, and even power used for good needs humility.

memory_verse.text: He has told you, O man, what is good; and what does the LORD require of you but to do justice, and to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God?

activity.title: Three Questions
steps: Retell the case of the man who won his debt but was caned anyway, and ask: was it fair, was it kind, was it humble?
Present a few everyday situations involving power: a team captain picking players, an older sibling left in charge, a group-chat admin.
In small groups, apply Micah’s three questions to each situation and decide what a fair, kind and humble response would be.
Ask each person to think of one place where they hold some power, and how they will use it this week.

weeks.summary: In 1903 the first communion is held at Akpap, and a new believer, Akom, says God’s revenge is sweeter than the consul’s. At Itu three young Africans, above all Mana, a former slave girl, start a church that soon numbers more than three hundred, and the chief Onoyom comes to faith through a homeless former teacher; Mary refuses to go back and the Church frees her to pioneer. The big idea: once we put our hand to the plough we keep going forward, and God often spreads the gospel through people nobody would put on a poster.

memory_verse.text: Jesus said to him, “No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God.”

activity.title: Unlikely Messengers
steps: As a group, list the people in this chapter through whom the gospel travelled: Mana, Esien, Effiom, a homeless former teacher and Onoyom.
Discuss why the chapter says the church at Itu owed its first life to a former slave girl rather than a Scottish missionary.
Talk honestly about the evidence that Mary’s work sometimes served the empire’s purposes, and what we can learn from that.
Have each person write down one new or uncomfortable step they have been putting off, and commit to take it this week.

weeks.summary: Past sixty and in constant pain, Mary keeps working at Ikpe, finding that strength comes once she begins, and she is honest that her faith is weak. She dies at Use on 13 January 1915, mourned as “Everybody’s Mother,” while the girls she raised fear they will now be counted as slaves; at her grave Mammy Fuller says one word: “Safe.” The big idea: God’s grace is sufficient, and his power is made perfect in our weakness.

memory_verse.text: But he said to me, “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.” Therefore I will boast all the more gladly of my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may rest upon me.

activity.title: Begin Anyway
steps: Read Mary’s words about beginning every day in pain and tiredness, and finding that the strength comes once she begins.
Discuss her prayer, “Lord, I believe, help Thou my unbelief,” and why honest weakness can be part of faith.
Look back over the thirteen weeks and invite each person to share one thing about Mary they want to remember.
Have each person write down a task they feel too tired or weak to begin, and commit to start it for ten minutes this week.
